analysis.one_liner: Lets students sue colleges in court instead of being forced into private arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was introduced in October 2023 and sat in the Senate education committee until the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Nearly all colleges make students sign enrollment contracts that force disputes into private arbitration and often ban class-action lawsuits. The bill would make those clauses unenforceable for schools that receive federal student aid, and would stop colleges from restricting students' ability to sue in court, including choosing where and how they sue. It was referred to the Senate education committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Students — and former students — who have disputes with their school over tuition, fraud, misrepresentation, or grades. Today they are typically locked into a private arbitration process chosen by the college, with no judge, no jury, no appeal, and no ability to join forces with other students in a class action. The bill would restore their right to take the school to court. All students at schools that participate in federal aid programs are covered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students disputing college bills or conduct

how_it_helps.text: The federal Arbitration Act would no longer apply to enrollment agreements between students and colleges, so mandatory arbitration clauses in those contracts could not be enforced.

Colleges receiving federal student aid would be barred from requiring or enforcing any restriction on students' ability to sue in court, including limits on jury trials, class actions, choice of law, or where a case is filed.
The changes would take effect one year after enactment, giving schools time to adjust their contracts.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities that participate in federal student aid, which would face lawsuits in open court instead of private arbitration, and the arbitration industry, which would lose enrollment-agreement disputes as a source of business.

drawbacks.text: Colleges argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper than court litigation, and that those savings help keep costs down; allowing courtroom suits and class actions could raise schools' legal exposure and, they contend, tuition. The bill's text contains no provision addressing tuition or school costs.

Because the bill applies to every institution of higher education that participates in federal aid, not just schools with records of abuse, it would eliminate arbitration even where a school has used it fairly and quickly to resolve small student disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and concrete: arbitration clauses leave students with a private process chosen and paid for by the college, with no public record and no appeal, and class-action bans prevent students with small dollar claims from banding together. The cost is higher litigation risk for schools, which could show up in tuition, though schools already operate under court exposure in many other areas of their business. On balance the bill trades a modest cost increase to institutions for a significant restoration of students' legal rights.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate's education committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there with no hearing, no vote, and no further action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on October 24, 2023, joined by eight Democratic senators including Blumenthal, Booker, Fetterman, Hirono, Markey, Reed, Warren, and Whitehouse.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was taken; the bill had no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges and universities that use mandatory arbitration clauses, and the arbitration industry, are better off: they keep the current system in which student disputes go to private arbitration chosen by the school rather than to court. Students' ability to sue colleges remains restricted.

for.name: Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar colleges from forcing students into arbitration.

for.name: 8 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: Blumenthal, Booker, Fetterman, Hirono, Markey, Reed, Warren, and Whitehouse.

against.name: Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to the committee; it received no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican senator joined, and the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities participating in federal student aid
industries.note: The bill would strip schools of their ability to enforce arbitration, class-action waivers, and venue limits in enrollment contracts, exposing them to lawsuits in open court. Schools currently benefit from resolving student disputes in a private forum they largely control.
Arbitration firms earn fees from disputes steered to them by contract; barring arbitration for student enrollment agreements would remove that stream of cases.
